solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Nasty odours — that’s disgusting bread!

indicators.note: something nasty is foul and messed up, so the letters beside it are jumbled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
UGH is the exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: Someone recoils from a smelly loaf and complains about the bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nasty odours' reads as a description of the smell, but 'Nasty' is the jumble signal; the exclamation 'that's disgusting' is rendered as a single grunt of distaste.
explanation.definitionFit: Sourdough is a kind of loaf leavened with a fermented starter culture instead of commercial yeast.

clue.text: Hears confession of hers: is Rev ultimately devious?

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the word is kept
devious means crooked or winding, so the letters take a twisted route into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the last letter of Rev

explanation.surface: A worshipper hears a woman's confession and wonders whether the vicar is being underhand.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon suggests a quotation from the confession, but 'hers: is' simply supplies letters. To shrive is an old word for a priest hearing confession and giving absolution.
explanation.definitionFit: Shriving is the archaic term for a priest listening to a penitent and granting absolution, so it is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Cat not wanting piano as musical instrument

indicators.note: not wanting something means doing without it, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: to cat is slang for to vomit
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly

explanation.surface: A cat that dislikes the piano takes up a different instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cat' is not the animal but the British slang verb meaning to be sick. A uke is the short form of ukulele.
explanation.definitionFit: Uke is the common shortening of ukulele, the small four-stringed guitar from Hawaii.

clue.text: Bitty food melts away, isn’t to be eaten

indicators.note: what is eaten goes inside, so one piece is swallowed by the other

blocks.note: to melt away is to fade out, to die
ain't is a colloquial form of isn't

explanation.surface: A plate of scraps disappears, though it was not meant to be eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitty food' is the definition: small delicate morsels. The colloquial contraction sits inside the word for fading away.
explanation.definitionFit: Dainties are small delicate treats, such as little cakes and sweets, served in bite-sized pieces.

clue.text: Encouraged to be purified with head obscured

indicators.note: when the head is hidden, the first letter disappears from view

blocks.note: to purge is to cleanse or purify

explanation.surface: Someone was pushed to undergo a cleansing ritual with a hood over their head.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for cleansed loses its opening letter to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To urge someone is to press or spur them on, which is a close synonym of encourage.

clue.text: A funny brother, exceptional person who has “a whale of a time”?

definitions.text: person who has “a whale of a time”?

blocks.note: Harpo was one of the Marx Brothers comedy team
a oner is a one-off, a remarkable individual; the following word 'person' serves both this piece and the definition

explanation.surface: A comedian's sibling is a remarkable character who always has a great time.
explanation.walkthrough: The Marx Brother is Harpo, the silent one. 'Oner' is British informal for someone unique. The definition takes the idiom 'a whale of a time' literally: a whaler's time is spent with whales.
explanation.definitionFit: A harpooner hunts whales with a barbed spear, so his working hours are literally a time spent among whales.

clue.text: Course of a good person holding firm

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: taken as written
ST is the abbreviation for saint, a good person
CO is short for company

explanation.surface: A decent person keeps a steady hand on the direction of their life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' is not a path but a racecourse; Ascot is the famous one in Berkshire, England, home of Royal Ascot.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a well-known English horse-racing venue, and racecourses are often simply called courses.

clue.text: Primate I listened to repeatedly

indicators.note: something listened to is taken in by ear, so what counts is how it sounds rather than its spelling

blocks.note: the letter I is said the same way as the old word for yes
the same sound once more

explanation.surface: An ape says it was paid attention to again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'I' twice and you hear the answer; AYE is an old and nautical word for yes, and the answer is a Madagascan lemur.
explanation.definitionFit: The aye-aye is a nocturnal lemur from Madagascar, and lemurs belong to the primate order.

clue.text: Male circle is broken with female finally out in priestly system

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so its letters are scattered and rebuilt
finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of the word is used
out means removed or excluded, so that letter is taken away

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
the last letter of female

explanation.surface: An all-male clergy is broken open once a woman is excluded from the church hierarchy.
explanation.walkthrough: Take one E out of MALE CIRCLE IS and rearrange the remaining eleven letters. 'Is' belongs to the fodder even though it looks like the verb of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Clericalism is a system or policy giving clergy power and influence, so it is a priestly way of ordering things.

clue.text: Fish — is one netted in that country?

indicators.note: something netted is caught inside a net, so these letters sit inside the other word

blocks.note: a tuna is a large sea fish
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A fisherman asks whether a catch is landed in some particular country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That country' is a slightly roundabout definition; the question mark covers the vagueness of pointing at a nation without naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunisia is a North African nation on the Mediterranean, and the clue simply points to it as a country.

clue.text: Slippery customer in group that’s dancing

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: an eel is famously slippery, and a slippery customer is an evasive person
a ring is a group of people, such as a crime ring

explanation.surface: A shifty character sneaks into a dance troupe.
explanation.walkthrough: A reel is a lively Scottish country dance, so reeling is dancing one.
explanation.definitionFit: To reel is to perform a reel, a brisk Scottish or Irish folk dance, so reeling means dancing it.

clue.text: See maiden being put off by head of faculty in school

indicators.note: to put someone off is to send them away, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: the Holy See, the Pope's seat, is in Rome
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
a dean heads a university faculty

explanation.surface: A dean discourages a young woman from studying at a school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is a bishop's seat, here the Holy See, Rome. Roedean is a well-known girls' boarding school near Brighton, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Roedean is an independent girls' boarding school on the Sussex coast, one of Britain's best-known private schools.

clue.text: Victor appears to be most important in call

blocks.note: V is Victor in the phonetic alphabet
stands for the verb meaning to be
to be IT is to be the most important thing

explanation.surface: The winner seems to be the key figure in a decision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victor' is the radio code word for V, not a winner, and 'it' is used as in 'this is it'.
explanation.definitionFit: A call can mean a short social visit, as when someone calls on a neighbour.

clue.text: Scrutinise noise over a Roman way somewhere in Europe

blocks.note: to scan is to examine closely
a din is a loud noise
taken as written
via is Latin for road or way

explanation.surface: An inspector investigates a racket on an old Roman road somewhere on the continent.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' just places the first pieces above the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Scandinavia is the northern region comprising Norway, Sweden and Denmark, so it is indeed a place in Europe.

clue.text: Greek tyrant insidiously bad, one beginning to lash out

indicators.note: bad suggests something gone wrong, so the letters are thrown into disorder
beginning points to the start, so only the first letter is taken
out means removed, so these letters are subtracted

blocks.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one
the first letter of lash

explanation.surface: A cruel Greek despot is sneakily wicked and starts lashing out at people.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I and L from INSIDIOUSLY and rearrange the nine letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: Dionysius the Elder was a ruthless ruler of ancient Syracuse, and 'tyrant' was the Greek title for such absolute rulers.

clue.text: National figure in America needing staff

blocks.note: the States is a common name for America
to staff a post is to man it

explanation.surface: A leading American politician needs employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like a noun but is the verb meaning to provide people for.
explanation.definitionFit: A statesman is a respected political leader, a prominent public person in the life of a nation.

clue.text: Avoid accepting points — there’s obscurity here

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece is received inside the other

blocks.note: to miss is to avoid
tines are the points or prongs of a fork or antler

explanation.surface: Someone dodges criticism and says the argument is unclear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Points' are not scores but the prongs of a fork.
explanation.definitionFit: Mistiness is haziness or lack of clarity, which is what obscurity means when vision or meaning is blurred.

clue.text: The old man needs two assistants

blocks.note: PA is short for personal assistant
two of them, so the same abbreviation comes again

explanation.surface: An elderly man requires a pair of helpers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old man' is slang for one's father, not an elderly person.
explanation.definitionFit: Papa is a familiar word for father, and 'the old man' is a colloquial term for one's dad.

clue.text: Man maybe cut short in trick move

indicators.note: cutting something short trims its end, so the final letter goes
in puts one piece inside another

blocks.note: the Isle of Man is an example of an isle; 'maybe' marks it as an example
a dodge is a trick or ruse

explanation.surface: A man's scheme is thwarted in a clever manoeuvre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, an island between Britain and Ireland, so 'Man maybe' is ISLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To dislodge something is to shift it out of place, so it is a specific kind of moving.

clue.text: Fusses about drink

indicators.note: about suggests turning round, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: ados are fusses or commotions

explanation.surface: Someone makes a big fuss over something to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning' but asks for the word to be turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Soda is a fizzy soft drink or carbonated water, a common beverage.

clue.text: Dog kept by wise person is better protected

indicators.note: something kept by another is held within it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: a seer is a prophet or sage
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A sage who keeps a guard dog is safer.
explanation.walkthrough: The mongrel sits inside the prophet.
explanation.definitionFit: Securer is the comparative of secure, meaning safer or more firmly protected.

clue.text: Overworking, Carol catches what can be caught

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: to carol is to sing joyfully
you catch a train

explanation.surface: An exhausted woman called Carol catches an illness.
explanation.walkthrough: Carol is the verb to sing, not a name, and 'what can be caught' suggests a cold but is transport.
explanation.definitionFit: Straining means exerting yourself to the limit, pushing too hard, which is overworking.

clue.text: Hard worker needing good support in the house?

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a rafter is a sloping beam supporting a roof

explanation.surface: A diligent employee needs a helpful partner at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support in the house' sounds emotional but is a roof beam. Graft is British slang for hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: In British informal usage, a grafter is someone who labours diligently, since graft means hard toil.

clue.text: Shop to take risk with minimal light?

blocks.note: to bet is to take a gamble
a ray is a thin beam, as in a ray of hope

explanation.surface: A store gambles by keeping its lighting dim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shop' is not a store but the British slang verb meaning to inform on someone to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: To shop someone is to inform on them to the authorities, which is an act of treachery against them.

clue.text: Study of chin is agreeable

blocks.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
genial in anatomy means relating to the chin

explanation.surface: Research into jaws turns out to be pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: The second piece uses the rare anatomical sense of genial, from the Greek for chin, not the everyday 'friendly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Congenial means pleasant and suited to one's taste, so it is a straightforward synonym for pleasing company.

clue.text: Optical device functioning gets one fooled

blocks.note: an LED is a light-emitting diode
a working machine is on

explanation.surface: A working gadget makes someone look foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: The device is an electronic light, and 'led on' is the phrasal verb for deceiving someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To be led on is to be deceived into false hopes, so someone led on has been duped.

clue.text: Lexicographer’s beginning with novel headword

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of Lexicographer's
Emma is a novel by Jane Austen

explanation.surface: A dictionary writer starts work on an entry with an unusual keyword.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like the adjective 'new' but is the book.
explanation.definitionFit: In a dictionary the lemma is the base form listed at the top of an entry, the headword under which variants appear.

clue.text: Trance is back, one knocking son out

indicators.note: knocking another out of its place means taking over its spot, so one letter replaces another

blocks.note: to back a car is to reverse it
I is the Roman numeral for one
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Someone announces that a hypnotic state has returned, and a boxer floors a young man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' is the verb meaning to drive backwards; the numeral for one knocks out the son's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverie is a dreamy state of absorbed thought, close to a trance or daydream.

clue.text: Follower of artistic style, pop, as it changed

indicators.note: something changed is altered, so the letters are put in a new arrangement

blocks.note: pop is an informal word for father
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A fan of an art movement follows pop art as it evolves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' is not pop art but father. Dada was an early twentieth-century anti-art movement.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dadaist is an adherent of Dada, the absurdist avant-garde movement in art and literature.

clue.text: Rocks in circle, odd ones invisible

indicators.note: if the odd-placed letters cannot be seen, only the even ones remain

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of circle

explanation.surface: Standing stones in a ring, some of them strangely hidden from view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocks' suggests stone circles, but it is the ice in a drink 'on the rocks'.
explanation.definitionFit: A drink served on the rocks comes with ice cubes, so rocks is a barroom term for frozen water.

clue.text: Yen after study to make dosh

blocks.note: to read a subject is to study it
Y is the symbol for the yen, Japan's currency

explanation.surface: Someone yearns, after their degree, to earn money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yen' tempts as longing but is the currency. Dosh and ready are both British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: The ready, or ready money, is British slang for cash available to spend, just as dosh is.

clue.text: Boy clear and always poetic, becoming an imitator of Shakespeare?

blocks.note: a son is a boy
to clear a sum is to net it as profit
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: A lad who is plain-spoken and forever lyrical turns into a copy of the Bard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear' means to make as profit, not transparent. The definition works because Shakespeare wrote 154 sonnets; the question mark admits the example.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonneteer writes sonnets, and anyone writing them follows in the path of Shakespeare's famous sequence.
